info.origin: Body and inferior ramus of the pubis
info.insertion: Pectineal line and upper linea aspera
info.action: Adducts the hip; assists flexion

info.origin: Body of the pubis, below the pubic crest
info.insertion: Middle third of the linea aspera
info.action: Adducts and flexes the hip
info.note: The most commonly injured adductor in kicking and change-of-direction sports.

info.origin: Inferior pubic ramus, ischial ramus and ischial tuberosity
info.insertion: Linea aspera and adductor tubercle of the femur
info.action: Adducts the hip; the hamstring part extends it
info.nerve: Obturator nerve and tibial part of the sciatic nerve

info.origin: Short head: coracoid process. Long head: supraglenoid tubercle
info.action: Flexes the elbow; supinates the forearm

info.origin: Long head: ischial tuberosity. Short head: linea aspera
info.action: Flexes the knee; long head extends the hip
info.nerve: Sciatic nerve (tibial and common fibular parts)
info.note: The long head is the most frequently strained hamstring in sprinting.

info.origin: Lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus
info.action: Flexes the elbow in a mid-prone position

info.desc: The heel bone, where the Achilles tendon and the plantar fascia attach.
The collarbone — the only bony strut connecting the arm to the trunk.

info.origin: Lateral clavicle, acromion and spine of the scapula
info.action: Abducts the shoulder; anterior fibres flex, posterior fibres extend

info.origin: Sacrum, iliac crest and lumbar/lower thoracic spinous processes
info.insertion: Ribs, vertebral processes and mastoid process
info.action: Extends and side-bends the spine

info.origin: Lateral epicondyle (common extensor origin)
info.action: Extends and radially deviates the wrist
info.nerve: Deep branch of the radial nerve (C7–C8)
info.note: Its origin is the usual site of lateral elbow tendinopathy ("tennis elbow").

info.origin: Lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus
info.action: Extends and radially deviates the wrist

info.origin: Lateral epicondyle and posterior ulna
info.action: Extends and ulnarly deviates the wrist

info.origin: Lateral epicondyle (common extensor origin)
info.action: Extends the fingers and wrist

info.origin: Lateral tibial condyle, fibula and interosseous membrane
info.action: Extends the toes; dorsiflexes the ankle

info.origin: Outer surfaces of ribs 5–12
info.insertion: Linea alba, pubic tubercle and anterior iliac crest
info.action: Flexes and rotates the trunk to the opposite side

structures.label: Femur

info.desc: The thigh bone — the longest and strongest bone in the body. The quadriceps, hamstrings and adductors act across it.

conditions: Knee ligament injuries (ACL, PCL, MCL, LCL attach here)

info.desc: The slender outer bone of the lower leg. It anchors the lateral collateral ligament, biceps femoris and fibularis muscles.

info.origin: Lower two-thirds of the lateral fibula
info.action: Everts and plantarflexes the foot

info.origin: Head and upper lateral fibula
info.insertion: Medial cuneiform and base of the first metatarsal
info.action: Everts and plantarflexes the foot; supports the arch

info.origin: Medial epicondyle, ulna and radius
info.insertion: Middle (superficial flexor) and distal (deep flexor) phalanges
info.action: Flex the fingers and wrist

info.origin: Medial epicondyle (common flexor origin)
info.action: Flexes and radially deviates the wrist

info.origin: Medial process of the calcaneal tuberosity
info.action: Flexes the toes; supports the arch

info.origin: Posterior tibia
info.action: Flexes the toes; plantarflexes and inverts the foot

info.origin: Medial and lateral femoral condyles
info.action: Plantarflexes the ankle; flexes the knee
info.note: Medial head strains are the classic "tennis leg".

info.origin: Posterior ilium, sacrum, coccyx and sacrotuberous ligament
info.insertion: Iliotibial tract and gluteal tuberosity of the femur
info.action: Extends and laterally rotates the hip

info.origin: Outer ilium between the anterior and posterior gluteal lines
info.action: Abducts the hip; keeps the pelvis level in single-leg stance

info.origin: Outer ilium between the anterior and inferior gluteal lines
info.action: Abducts and medially rotates the hip

info.origin: Body and inferior ramus of the pubis
info.action: Adducts the hip; flexes the knee

info.desc: The ilium, ischium and pubis fused into one bone. Origin of the hamstrings, adductors, glutes and rectus femoris.
The upper arm bone, from the shoulder socket to the elbow.

info.origin: Iliac fossa
info.insertion: Lesser trochanter of the femur (with psoas)
info.action: Flexes the hip

info.origin: Infraspinous fossa of the scapula
info.insertion: Middle facet of the greater tubercle
info.action: Laterally rotates the shoulder

info.origin: Transverse processes of C1–C4
info.action: Elevates the scapula; side-bends the neck

info.origin: Inner surface of the obturator membrane and surrounding bone
info.action: Laterally rotates the hip; stabilises the femoral head

info.origin: Medial epicondyle (common flexor origin)
info.action: Flexes the wrist; tenses the palmar fascia

info.desc: The kneecap — a sesamoid bone in the quadriceps tendon that increases its lever arm. Its cartilage surface is the source of patellofemoral pain.

info.origin: Clavicle, sternum and costal cartilages 1–6
info.insertion: Lateral lip of the intertubercular groove of the humerus
info.action: Adducts, medially rotates and flexes the shoulder

info.origin: Ribs 3–5
info.action: Draws the scapula forward and down

info.origin: Anterior surface of the sacrum
info.action: Laterally rotates the extended hip; abducts the flexed hip

info.origin: Lateral supracondylar line of the femur
info.insertion: Calcaneus, medial to the Achilles tendon
info.action: Weakly plantarflexes the ankle and flexes the knee

info.origin: Lateral femoral condyle
info.insertion: Posterior tibia above the soleal line
info.action: Unlocks the extended knee by medially rotating the tibia

info.origin: Distal anterior ulna
info.action: Pronates the forearm

info.origin: Bodies and transverse processes of T12–L5
info.action: Flexes the hip; stabilises the lumbar spine

info.origin: Anterior inferior iliac spine (straight head) and ilium above the acetabulum (reflected head)
info.insertion: Base of patella, then tibial tuberosity via the patellar ligament
info.action: Extends the knee; flexes the hip
info.note: The only quadriceps muscle crossing both hip and knee, which is why it is the one most often strained — typically while kicking or sprinting.

info.origin: Greater trochanter and lateral lip of the linea aspera
info.action: Extends the knee

info.origin: Intertrochanteric line and medial lip of the linea aspera
info.action: Extends the knee; its oblique fibres help stabilise the patella

info.origin: Anterior and lateral surfaces of the femoral shaft
info.insertion: Deep surface of the quadriceps tendon
info.action: Extends the knee
info.note: Lies directly on the femur — the muscle most often involved in a deep "dead leg" contusion.

info.desc: The lateral forearm bone, which rotates around the ulna in pronation and supination.

info.origin: Spinous processes of T2–T5
info.action: Retracts and stabilises the scapula

info.desc: Five fused vertebrae forming the back of the pelvis and the sacroiliac joints.

info.origin: Anterior superior iliac spine
info.action: Flexes, abducts and laterally rotates the hip; flexes the knee
info.note: The longest muscle in the body.

info.desc: The shoulder blade — origin of the rotator cuff and a moving base for the arm.

info.origin: Ischial tuberosity
info.action: Flexes the knee; extends the hip; medially rotates the tibia
info.nerve: Tibial part of the sciatic nerve (L5–S2)

info.origin: Ischial tuberosity
info.action: Flexes the knee; extends the hip; medially rotates the tibia
info.nerve: Tibial part of the sciatic nerve (L5–S2)

info.origin: Outer surfaces of ribs 1–8
info.insertion: Anterior medial border of the scapula
info.action: Protracts and upwardly rotates the scapula

info.origin: Soleal line of the tibia and upper posterior fibula
info.action: Plantarflexes the ankle, especially with the knee bent

info.origin: Manubrium of the sternum and medial clavicle
info.insertion: Mastoid process of the temporal bone
info.action: Flexes the neck; rotates the head to the opposite side

info.origin: Subscapular fossa
info.action: Medially rotates the shoulder

info.origin: Lateral epicondyle and supinator crest of the ulna
info.action: Supinates the forearm
info.nerve: Deep branch of the radial nerve (C6)

info.origin: Supraspinous fossa of the scapula
info.insertion: Superior facet of the greater tubercle
info.action: Initiates abduction; centres the humeral head
info.note: The rotator cuff tendon most often affected by tendinopathy and tears.

info.desc: Transmits body weight from the tibia to the foot and forms the ankle joint.

info.origin: Inferior angle of the scapula
info.insertion: Medial lip of the intertubercular groove
info.action: Adducts, medially rotates and extends the shoulder

info.origin: Lateral border of the scapula
info.insertion: Inferior facet of the greater tubercle
info.action: Laterally rotates the shoulder

info.desc: The shin bone and main weight-bearing bone of the lower leg. The cruciate and collateral ligaments of the knee attach to it (not modelled in the source data).

info.origin: Lateral tibial condyle and upper lateral tibia
info.insertion: Medial cuneiform and base of the first metatarsal
info.action: Dorsiflexes and inverts the foot

info.origin: Posterior tibia, fibula and interosseous membrane
info.action: Inverts and plantarflexes the foot; supports the medial arch

info.origin: Occipital bone, nuchal ligament and spinous processes C7–T12
info.insertion: Lateral clavicle, acromion and spine of the scapula
info.action: Elevates, retracts, depresses and upwardly rotates the scapula

info.origin: Long head: infraglenoid tubercle. Lateral and medial heads: posterior humerus
info.action: Extends the elbow; long head extends the shoulder

info.desc: The medial forearm bone; its olecranon forms the point of the elbow.
The longest ligament of the sole, running from the calcaneus to the cuboid and metatarsal bases. It supports the lateral longitudinal arch.
The Achilles tendon — the thickest, strongest tendon in the body. It joins gastrocnemius and soleus to the calcaneus and stores energy with every stride.
A thin ligament from the styloid process of the temporal bone to the hyoid.
The intermediate tendon of the digastric muscle, looped to the hyoid bone.
A fibrous band forming the roof of the carpal tunnel, through which the median nerve and finger flexor tendons pass.
A fibrous sheet binding the radius and ulna, transferring load between them and giving muscles an attachment surface.
A fibrous sheet between the tibia and fibula that separates the front and back compartments of the lower leg.

Runs from the inner wall of the lateral femoral condyle to the front of the tibial plateau, between the tibial spines. It stops the tibia sliding forward and controls rotation — the ligament torn in pivoting and landing injuries.
info.placement: Tibial centre at 43 % of the plateau’s front-to-back depth; femoral centre on the lateral notch wall; inclined about 50° to the plateau.

refs.t: Hwang et al. 2012, ACL femoral footprint anatomy: systematic review (Arthroscopy)
Sehmi et al. 2022, Morphometry of the ACL tibial footprint (Natl J Clin Anat)
Scheffler et al. 2018, 3D MRI of the intact ACL footprints (KSSTA)

info.desc: The strongest knee ligament. It runs from the inner wall of the medial femoral condyle to the back of the tibia and stops the tibia sagging backwards — injured by a blow to the front of a bent knee or a fall onto it.
info.placement: Femoral footprint on the lateral wall of the medial condyle (front of the notch); tibial footprint in the posterior intercondylar fossa about 1 cm below the joint line.

info.desc: A broad, flat band on the inner knee from the femur to the tibia. It resists the knee being pushed inwards (valgus) and is the most commonly sprained knee ligament.
info.placement: Femoral attachment 3.2 mm proximal and 4.8 mm posterior to the medial epicondyle; tibial attachments ~16 mm and ~61 mm below the joint line.

refs.t: LaPrade et al. 2007, The anatomy of the medial part of the knee (JBJS Am)
Wijdicks et al. 2009, Radiographic identification of the primary medial knee structures (JBJS Am)

info.desc: A cord-like ligament on the outer knee from the lateral femoral epicondyle to the head of the fibula. It resists the knee bowing outwards (varus).
info.placement: Femoral attachment 1.4 mm proximal and 3.1 mm posterior to the lateral epicondyle; fibular attachment on the lateral fibular head, ~8 mm behind its front edge.

refs.t: LaPrade et al. 2003, The posterolateral attachments of the knee (Am J Sports Med)

info.desc: C-shaped fibrocartilage cushion on the inner tibial plateau. Wider at the back than the front, and anchored to the MCL, which makes it less mobile and more often torn than the lateral meniscus.
info.placement: Width ~9 mm (anterior horn), ~10 mm (body) and ~15 mm (posterior horn); ~5–6 mm high at the rim.

refs.t: Study of the morphometry and histology of human menisci, 2025 (Acta Med Int)
Chaware et al. 2023, Morphology and morphometry of human knee menisci (Cureus)

info.desc: Almost circular fibrocartilage cushion on the outer tibial plateau, of even width, and more mobile than the medial meniscus.
info.placement: Width ~10–11 mm throughout; ~5–6 mm high at the rim.

refs.t: Study of the morphometry and histology of human menisci, 2025 (Acta Med Int)
Chaware et al. 2023, Morphology and morphometry of human knee menisci (Cureus)

info.desc: Links the lower pole of the kneecap to the tibial tuberosity and transmits all the quadriceps’ force to the shin. The site of "jumper’s knee".
info.placement: From the inferior pole of the patella to the centre of the tibial tuberosity; ~25–30 mm wide.

info.desc: A flat band from the front of the lateral malleolus to the neck of the talus. The first — and most often — injured ligament when the ankle rolls inwards.
info.placement: Anterior border of the lateral malleolus to the lateral talar neck.

info.desc: A cord from the tip of the lateral malleolus down and back to the outer calcaneus. Usually torn after the ATFL in more severe inversion sprains.
info.placement: Tip of the lateral malleolus to the lateral calcaneus, running posterior-inferior.

info.desc: The strongest of the lateral ankle ligaments, running horizontally from the malleolar fossa to the back of the talus. Rarely injured except in dislocations.
info.placement: Malleolar fossa of the fibula to the posterolateral talar tubercle.

info.desc: A strong fan-shaped ligament from the medial malleolus to the navicular, calcaneus and talus. It resists the ankle rolling outwards.
info.placement: Medial malleolus fanning to the navicular tuberosity, sustentaculum tali and posterior talus (superficial bands shown).

info.desc: A thick band under the sole from the heel to the base of the toes. It supports the arch and stiffens the foot for push-off; heel pain arises at its origin.
info.placement: Medial calcaneal tubercle fanning to the five metatarsal heads.

info.desc: The anterior bundle of the elbow’s inner ligament, from the medial epicondyle to the sublime tubercle of the ulna. It resists valgus stress and is the ligament rebuilt in "Tommy John" surgery.
info.placement: Medial epicondyle to the sublime tubercle; ~29 mm long.

refs.t: Moen et al. 2023, Radiographic description of soft-tissue attachments around the elbow (ABJS)

info.desc: Passes under the acromion to the top of the greater tuberosity. The rotator cuff tendon most often affected by tendinopathy and tears.
info.placement: Superior facet of the greater tuberosity; footprint ~23 × 16 mm.

refs.t: Curtis et al. 2006, The insertional footprint of the rotator cuff (Arthroscopy)
Mochizuki et al. 2008, Humeral insertion of the supraspinatus and infraspinatus (JBJS Am)

info.desc: Wraps over the back of the humeral head to the middle facet of the greater tuberosity; its footprint extends further forward than once thought.
info.placement: Middle facet of the greater tuberosity; footprint ~29 × 19 mm.

refs.t: Curtis et al. 2006, The insertional footprint of the rotator cuff (Arthroscopy)
Mochizuki et al. 2008, Humeral insertion of the supraspinatus and infraspinatus (JBJS Am)

info.desc: Inserts on the lowest facet of the greater tuberosity and helps rotate the arm outwards.
info.placement: Inferior facet of the greater tuberosity; footprint ~29 × 21 mm.

refs.t: Curtis et al. 2006, The insertional footprint of the rotator cuff (Arthroscopy)

info.desc: The largest cuff tendon, crossing the front of the shoulder to the lesser tuberosity. It rotates the arm inwards and holds the humeral head forward-stable.
info.placement: Lesser tuberosity beside the bicipital groove; footprint ~40 × 20 mm.

refs.t: Curtis et al. 2006, The insertional footprint of the rotator cuff (Arthroscopy)
